newsitem.title: JAPAN: Economy can probably bear fiscal tightening -- BOJ.
newsitem.headline: Economy can probably bear fiscal tightening -- BOJ.

text.p: Kengo Inoue, an adviser to the Bank of Japan's governor, said on Thursday that the Japanese economy can probably withstand adverse effects from fiscal tightening, but this would carry some risks.

Asked how he views a newspaper report that the BOJ may adjust its monetary policy before assessing the possible impact of a planned rise in the consumption tax, he said: "That was quoted rather wrongly." He did not elaborate on the remark.
"There is a good chance that the economy can withstand that (fiscal tightening) shock, but we are not sure. There are some risks that it might not," he told Reuters Financial Television.
"That risk as of now is probably bigger than the risk of inflation," Inoue said.
The Japanese government has said it will cut public spending, including public works spending, as much as possible to reduce Japan's huge budget deficit.

Asked if a reevaluation of the BOJ's monetary policy is possible before April 1, Inoue said: "We are evaluating policy every day... That's a very academic question, and I cannot answer." Asked about the prospects for self-sustainable recovery, Inoue said: "We can never be 100 percent sure. It all depends on what economic data we get in the coming months."
Inoue explained that there are some risks that the recovery may not turn out to be sustainable, but this judgement may change in the coming months.
"As of now, as the governor said, the priority is to address the risk of the economy not being strong enough," he said.
Inflationary risks at the moment are small, he added.

Inoue said the speed of the recovery is slow, but added that one must look at the nature of the recovery -- whether it is purely supported by the government's economic policies or whether it is autonomous.
He said that the more autonomous the recovery is, the better the chances for a self-sustainable recovery, but the BOJ is not 100 percent certain about the prospects.

"Judging from the fact that many corporations, including small corporations, added to their investment plans, (this) might mean that they are slowly getting more confident about the future," Inoue said.
